title: The literal meanings of world foods

entries.note: The last course, eaten after the table has been cleared of everything else; it comes from the same serving verb as [[same-root:just deserts]], and is unrelated to [[unrelated:desert]].
Means what you deserve, almost an eggcorn because people think it means being served [[same-root:dessert]]; both come from the same serving verb.
Comes from a different Latin root, meaning to join together or put in a row; a deserted place is severed from humanity, unrelated to [[unrelated:dessert]].
Literally a pick-me-up, from its coffee or liqueur; a claimed 1800s Treviso brothel origin is doubted because the word isn't recorded until the 1980s; possibly based on [[from?:zuppa inglese]].
The local Treviso dialect word for a madam, used in the brothel origin story of [[see:tiramisu]].
An Italian take on English [[see:trifle]], with liqueur-soaked sponge, custard and fruit, and one theory for the origin of [[gave?:tiramisu]].
Rob's nan's sherry trifle had layers of sherry-soaked sponge, jelly or jam, custard and whipped cream; in America almost anything layered in a clear dish counts.
In British English it means liquid cream whipped by hand, whereas Americans use the term for what the British call [[see:squirty cream]].
The British name for the aerosol cream that Americans call [[see:whipped cream]].
A contraction of 'some more', popularised by a 1927 Girl Scouts cookbook; it was preceded by [[see:marshmallow marguerites]] and the [[see:Mallomar]].
Named after the dietary reformer [[from:Sylvester Graham]]; originally sweetened with molasses, mentioned by Herman Melville in 1852, and later made by [[see:Nabisco]].
American Presbyterian minister and dietary reformer who promoted temperance, vegetarianism and bland whole-grain food, and who gave his name to the [[see:graham cracker]].
Coarsely ground flour named after [[from:Sylvester Graham]].
The followers of [[from:Sylvester Graham]], and one of the first vegetarian movements in America.
Short for the National Biscuit Company, which made the [[see:graham cracker]] what it is today and released the [[see:Mallomar]].
An earlier version of [[gave:s'mores]]: butter and marshmallow spread on a saltine cracker, toasted, and served with hot chocolate or tea.
Released by [[see:Nabisco]] in 1913: a graham cracker topped with marshmallow and covered in chocolate, one of the forerunners of [[see:s'mores]].
Not named after Germany but after [[from:Samuel German]], whose dark baking chocolate was used in the cake with its coconut-pecan frosting.
English-American chocolate maker whose dark baking chocolate gave its name to [[see:German chocolate cake]].
A chocolatey cake named after the Black Forest in Germany; its German name is Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte.
Not from [[unrelated:braten]] (to roast), as is often thought, but from a Middle High German term meaning diced meat.
The German word for roasting, as in [[see:sauerbraten]], and wrongly thought to be the source of [[unrelated:bratwurst]].
Given as an example of a word that does contain [[from:braten]].
A fat boiled sausage named not after a goat but after [[from:bock beer]], which it is served with in Berlin and Bavaria.
A seasonal dark lager, perhaps named after goats because it makes you giddy, or from [[from?:Einbeck]], which a Bavarian accent renders as 'ein Bock'.
A Hanseatic trading city where [[see:bock beer]] was supposedly first brewed in the 14th century; in a Bavarian accent it sounds like 'ein Bock'.
What most people in England call the sausage that Americans call a [[see:wiener]].
Means a sausage from Vienna; it was invented in Frankfurt, so in Vienna it is called a [[see:frankfurter]].
A small boiled sausage invented in Frankfurt; in Vienna it is called a Frankfurter, while in Frankfurt it is called a Vienna sausage, or [[see:wiener]].
A German suffix meaning 'from a place', as in [[see:wiener]], [[see:frankfurter]] and [[see:hamburger]].
A steak from Hamburg, given as an example of the German [[see:-er]] suffix.
Simply means blood sausage.
A chunky parboiled sausage named from knacken, to crackle, as the sausage bursts; Americans often say knockwurst, which Rob calls as wrong as a word can be.
The OED shows it can also mean a snap, and that it comes from the same Germanic source as [[same-root:knackwurst]].
Means something that has been cut, much like a cutlet.
A word one language lends to another, which then lends it back, as with [[see:katsu]].
A [[see:boomerang word]]: Japanese katsuretsu renders English [[from:cutlet]] to fit Japanese syllable rules, and English borrowed it back as in chicken katsu.
English beer reshaped to fit Japanese syllable structure, an example alongside [[see:toire]] and [[see:katsu]].
English toilet adapted to Japanese syllable rules, an example alongside [[see:bīru]] and [[see:katsu]].
Vietnamese noodle soup invented under French occupation; its name may come from French [[from?:pot-au-feu]] or from Chinese words like [[from?:fàn]], or both.
A Sino-Korean word that has changed over time; the word it comes from literally means submerged vegetables.
Literally kimchi soup, since jjigae just means soup.
A Korean rice dish served in a hot stone bowl; despite its fun name, it just means mixed rice.
Means fire meat.
Means stir-fried noodles; mein, mian or men in an East Asian dish name usually signals noodles, as in [[see:lo mein]] and [[see:ramen]].
Simply means tossed noodles.
A Japanese take on a Chinese name, meaning pulled noodles; the -men means noodles, as in [[same-root:chow mein]].
From Chinese gong bao, meaning palace guardian, the title of [[from:Ding Baozhen]], a Qing official who loved the spicy chicken-and-peanut dish.
Qing dynasty official who was particularly fond of the dish believed to be named after him, [[see:kung pao chicken]].
No one knows what it means; proposals include gratitude, barely fills your stomach and close to the heart, probably because it comes from a longer phrase.
Hand-pulled noodles from Shaanxi, named for the sound of dough hitting the counter; written with perhaps the most complex Chinese character in use, with 58 strokes.
The word for the pounded rice paste that mochi is made from, shortened from the name of the product.
The practice of making [[see:mochi]].
Literally vinegar rice, so without rice it is technically not sushi but perhaps [[see:sashimi]].
Fresh fish served on its own, with no rice, as opposed to [[see:sushi]].
A slab of rice topped with a sliver of fish; it means grip or press, after how the chef shapes it by hand.
Battered, deep-fried seafood and vegetables from Nagasaki; it comes from Latin [[from:tempora]], meaning times, referring to the [[see:Ember days]] of Portuguese Jesuit missionaries.
Days when Catholics ate fish rather than meat, the 'times' behind the name [[see:tempura]].
A Louisiana stew thickened with roux, okra or [[see:filé powder]]; its name comes from an African word for okra, possibly a Bantu one.
In Creole cooking, the trio of celery, bell peppers and onions.
A thickener made from the sassafras tree and contributed by the Choctaw; filé is a French term related to [[same-root:filament]], meaning ropy or threadlike.
A one-pot rice dish probably named after Provençal [[from?:jambonette]], possibly linked to French [[from?:jambe]], and influenced by a French word for a mishmash; it sounds like [[see:jumble]].
Compared with [[see:jambalaya]] as a similar one-pot rice dish.
Probably not a coincidence that [[see:jambalaya]] sounds like it, which may have helped the word survive in English.
Also called Hopping Johnny, an American dish of bacon, rice and peas that was sometimes considered the same as [[see:jambalaya]].
Simply French for smothered, since sauce is poured over the dish; usually made with [[see:crawfish]] or [[see:crawdads]].
A regional name for [[see:crayfish]], used in [[see:étouffée]].
Another regional name for [[see:crayfish]].
From Old French [[from:escrevis]], reshaped to sound more English, ending in 'fish' even though it isn't one.
Deep-fried cornmeal balls, and in Britain a type of shoe; the story goes that hunters fed them to dogs to keep them quiet, but the origin is unknown.
A messy ground-beef sandwich supposedly named after [[from?:José Abeal Otero]]'s Havana bar; [[see:Ernest Hemingway]] reportedly got [[see:Joe Russell]] to rename his Key West bar Sloppy Joe's.
Named after Bologna, like [[same-root:bologna]], and compared with the [[see:sloppy joe]].
Spelled like the name of the city it is named after, though Americans pronounce it 'baloney'.
A Cuban bar owner nicknamed Sloppy Joe who, in 1917 in Havana, supposedly created the ground beef sandwich that became the [[see:sloppy joe]].
A regular at the Havana bar who supposedly convinced [[see:Joe Russell]] to rename his Key West bar Sloppy Joe's in 1937.
A Key West bar owner who renamed his bar Sloppy Joe's at [[see:Ernest Hemingway]]'s urging, and who also served the [[see:sloppy joe]] sandwich.
An eponym: improvised in 1943 by [[from:Ignacio Anaya]] at the Victory Club for [[see:Mamie Finan]] and officers' wives, who called them Nacho's special.
A maître d', nicknamed Nacho (a pet form of Ignacio), who invented [[see:nachos]], was promoted to chef and later opened his own restaurant.
A regular at the Victory Club who asked what the new dish of [[see:nachos]] should be called.
Probably a variation on [[from?:pita]]; some Italian sources suggest a word meaning clamp, pound or stamp instead.
A Greek and Latin word for a piece of bread, from Greek [[from:peptos]], cooked, and related to [[same-root:bite]]; probably the source of [[gave?:pizza]].
Said to be related to [[same-root:pita]] going back to Proto-Indo-European.
Means a trouser leg or stocking, because it is stuffed like a foot in a sock, the same idea as French [[equivalent:chausson]].
French for soft footwear such as baby booties and for a type of pastry, related to [[same-root:chaussette]], [[same-root:chaussure]] and [[same-root:chaussée]].
French for sock, one of several foot-related words related to [[same-root:chausson]].
French for shoe, related to [[same-root:chausson]].
French for the pavement you walk along, related to [[same-root:chausson]].
Sort of means a stick; the story goes that it was designed to fit down soldiers' trousers so they could carry bread to war.
One of the Italian pasta suffixes (-ini, -elli, -illi, -etti, -ine, -elle) meaning something small, in contrast to [[see:-oni]].
Along with -one and -otti, the Italian suffix meaning something big, in contrast to [[see:-ini]].
An Italian suffix added to a pasta's name when it has been badly made, as in [[see:spaghettacci]].
Badly made, overcooked [[from:spaghetti]], formed with the suffix [[from:-acci]].
Literally means little strings.
Means little cut things; taglia is related to [[same-root:tailor]].
Ultimately just means a cutter, and is related to the taglia in [[same-root:tagliatelle]].
Means little bells.
Shell-shaped pasta, like a [[see:conch]], whose correct pronunciation Jess only recently discovered.
The reason Jess pronounced [[see:conchiglie]] as she did.
Bow-tie pasta, whose name is Italian for butterflies.
Means little tongues, reportedly referring to snake tongues rather than human ones.
Doesn't mean little anything; it means gobble up, from the Italian verb [[from:pappare]], to eat something up.
Spiral pasta meaning little spindles, discussed earlier in an episode on airplane anatomy alongside [[same-root:fuselage]].
Means the spindle in French, discussed in an earlier episode on airplane anatomy and linked to [[same-root:fusilli]].
Related to [[same-root:pen]], meaning a quill or feather, which the pasta resembles; it comes as [[see:penne rigate]] or [[see:penne lisce]].
Related to [[same-root:penne]].
Ridged penne, since rigate means striped; the ridges help the sauce cling, unlike [[see:penne lisce]].
Smooth penne without the ridges of [[see:penne rigate]].
Means knuckles; a pasta made with potato, semolina or wheat flour whose spelling makes it hard to pronounce.
Origin unknown; theories include little turnips or a word for a robe, but early ravioli were meatballs, sometimes with no pasta wrapping at all.
